lead: A sorting network is a fixed pattern of compare-exchange units wired between input and output wires. The pattern never changes with the data, so it suits hardware and SIMD machines. Parallel time is the network's depth: the longest chain of comparators from input to output. Networks sort in routers, GPUs and merge hardware.
prereq: You need Chapter 2.3 for broadcast, Chapter 2.4 for pivot selection, and Unit 1 for mesh and hypercube networks.

blocks.text: A comparator has two input wires and two output wires. An ascending comparator puts the smaller key on the top wire; a descending comparator reverses them. A sorting network is a fixed list of comparators, the same for every input: no branches, no data-dependent indices.
Size is the comparator count. Depth is the longest chain from input to output; all comparators in one stage run together, so depth is parallel time.

blocks.where: T is parallel time; depth is the number of stages on the longest path; t_cmp is the delay of one comparator.

blocks.text: 0-1 principle: a network sorts every input if and only if it sorts all 2ⁿ inputs of 0s and 1s. For n = 4, test all 16 binary inputs instead of testing a few sample key arrays.

Odd-even transposition sort on a linear array of n processors alternates phases. Even phase compares (0,1), (2,3), ...; odd phase compares (1,2), (3,4), .... Run n phases, about n/2 comparators in parallel each, so time is O(n) with n processors.
Insertion sort on a linear array pipelines keys through in O(n) phases.

A bitonic sequence first increases and then decreases (cyclically, only one rise and one fall). Bitonic sort pairs elements with comparators in alternating directions to build bitonic sequences of length 2, 4, 8, …, then merges each bitonic sequence into a sorted one. For n = 2^k, depth is k(k+1)/2 = O(log² n), size O(n log² n).
Odd-even merge sort has the same depth k(k+1)/2 and the same O(n log² n) size, with a smaller comparator count, but its merge network is more intricate than the bitonic merge.

Enumeration sort ranks each key by counting smaller keys, using about n²/2 comparisons. On a CRCW machine with n² processors all pairs are compared in one step. The n comparison results of each key are then added, for example by a tree in O(log n) steps, giving O(log n) time with n² processors (O(n) time if only n processors are used).
Parallel quicksort chooses a pivot, splits keys into smaller and larger sets, and recurses on both sets in parallel. Balanced pivots keep the recursion shallow; Chapter 2.4 covers pivot selection.

Hyperquicksort runs on a hypercube. Each processor sorts its block and broadcasts its local median. The median of these p local medians is chosen as the pivot and broadcast along the hypercube. Each processor then splits its own block around the pivot and sends one part to the partner in the other subcube, so each half holds about n/2 keys even though the split is not exact. The cube dimension drops by one. Expected time is O((n/p) log(n/p) + log² p) for p processors.
Mesh sort for n² keys on an n×n mesh: snake-order rows, sort rows, sort columns, sort rows. This takes O(n) steps.
Parallel merging on CREW/EREW: binary-search each key of A in B and each key of B in A to find its rank. Every key then writes once to its output position; each rank costs O(log n).

examples.question: Sort keys [3, 1, 4, 2] with the 4-input bitonic network. Give the array after each stage, the depth, the comparator count, and compare with odd-even transposition sort.
steps: Stage 1: (0,1) ascending turns 3,1 into 1,3; (2,3) descending keeps 4,2. Array [1, 3, 4, 2].
Stage 2: (0,2) ascending keeps 1,4; (1,3) ascending turns 3,2 into 2,3. Array [1, 2, 4, 3].
Depth 3, size 6 comparators. Odd-even transposition on 4 keys needs 4 phases and 6 comparators, so bitonic keeps the same size with one stage fewer.
examples.answer: Sorted [1, 2, 3, 4]; bitonic depth 3 with 6 comparators; odd-even transposition depth 4 with 6 comparators.

traps: Testing one input and declaring the network correct. Use the 0-1 principle: all 2ⁿ binary inputs.
Reporting size when asked for depth. Depth is parallel time; size is total work.
Forgetting the descending comparator in the first bitonic stage. The first half rises, the second falls.
Saying odd-even transposition needs n/2 phases. It needs n phases for n keys.
On CREW, enumeration sort cannot write equal ranks in one step; the CRCW assumption matters.

quiz.q: Define a sorting network and its depth.
quiz.a: A fixed pattern of comparators independent of the input. Depth is the longest comparator chain from input to output.

quiz.q: Why is depth, not size, the parallel time?
quiz.a: Comparators in one stage run together. Size measures total work; depth counts sequential stages.

quiz.q: An 8-input bitonic network has n = 8 = 2³. Find its depth.
Keys [3, 1, 2] use enumeration sort. Give each key's rank.
quiz.a: Ranks count smaller keys: 3→2, 1→0, 2→1. Sorted order is 1, 2, 3.

quiz.q: Why does the 0-1 principle avoid testing all n! orders?
quiz.a: If a network fails on any input, a threshold on that input gives a 0/1 input that also fails. So all binary inputs passing proves all orders pass.

quiz.q: What pivot does hyperquicksort use and why?
quiz.a: The median of the p local medians. It makes each processor's split roughly balanced, so the two subcubes carry roughly equal work.

quiz.q: Compare bitonic sort and odd-even transposition for 8 keys.
quiz.a: Bitonic: depth 6, size 24 comparators. Odd-even transposition: 8 phases, n(n−1)/2 = 28 comparators. Bitonic is shallower and, for n ≥ 4, uses no more comparators, far fewer as n grows.

beyond: Not for the exam. Sorting networks reappear in FPGA and ASIC sorters, GPU bitonic kernels, and switch fabrics. Batcher's odd-even merge is a common hardware merge. Search terms: Batcher odd-even mergesort, bitonic sort CUDA, sorting network verification, 0-1 principle.
